question: Which choices in the SFT data pipeline (question source, mixing, filtering, deduplication and repeated sampling, answer filtering, teacher) produce the strongest open reasoning dataset for distilling long chain-of-thought into a 7B model?
hypothesis: Implied: standard data-curation heuristics (diversity, answer verification, using the strongest teacher, pretraining-style filters) may not transfer to reasoning SFT, so each pipeline step should be tested by downstream performance; the intro says the project aims at 'challenging preexisting notions of data quality'.
contributions: More than 1,000 controlled ablation experiments over six pipeline steps (question sourcing, mixing, question filtering, deduplication and multiple sampling, answer filtering, teacher) across math, code and science.
OpenThoughts3-1.2M, a 1.2M-example open SFT reasoning dataset, and OpenThinker3-7B, a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct finetune that is state of the art among open-data 7B/8B reasoning models.

Five stated insights: multiple answers per question scale a data source by at least 16x; a better-scoring model is not necessarily a better teacher; no verification or answer filtering method gave significant gains; 1-2 high-quality question sources beat many; LLM-based difficulty or response-length question filters beat fastText or embedding filters.
Release of datasets, models and (promised) code at openthoughts.ai.

method.summary: For each pipeline step the authors generate 31,600 question-answer pairs per strategy (teacher DeepSeek-R1 unless stated), finetune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and pick the strategy with the best average over 8 benchmarks, then proceed to the next step. The winning recipe (best sources, LLM-based question filter, 16x teacher sampling, no answer filter, QwQ-32B teacher) is scaled to 1.2M examples (850K math, 250K code, 100K science) to train OpenThinker3-7B.
method.task: Supervised fine-tuning data curation for long chain-of-thought reasoning (math, code, science) by distillation from a reasoning teacher

results.claim: OpenThinker3-7B beats DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B by 12.4 points on average across the 12 benchmark tasks.
results.setup: OpenThinker3-7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct finetuned on OpenThoughts3-1.2M, SFT) versus DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (800K, not trained by the authors); Evalchemy, temperature 0.7, top_p 1.0, 32,768 max new tokens; Table 1 averages 55.3 versus 42.9.
results.quote: outperforming the R1-Distill-7B model by 12.4 points on average across 12 tasks

results.claim: On held-out AIME 2025, OpenThinker3-7B scores 53.3 against 38.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
results.setup: AIME25 was held out of all pipeline decisions; mean over 10 iterations at temperature 0.7, 32,768 max new tokens; baseline model trained on 800K samples by DeepSeek.
results.table: Table 1, row AIME25, columns OpenThoughts3-7B (53.3) and DS-R1-Qwen-7B (38.0)
results.note: Table 1 also lists Skywork-7B at 50.7 and AceReason-7B at 48.0 on AIME25 (RL models). The same 53.3 appears in Table 2.

results.claim: OpenThinker3-7B outperforms the next-best open-data model (Nemotron-Nano-8B) by 2.1 points on average.
results.setup: Table 1 averages 55.3 versus 53.2; 7B and 8B open-data models only.
results.quote: outperforming the next-best open-data model (Nemotron-Nano-8B) by 2.1 points
results.note: On GPQA-D, OpenR1-Distill-7B scores 58.9 against 53.7 for OpenThinker3-7B in Table 1; the lead is in the average.

results.claim: Using QwQ-32B as teacher beats DeepSeek-R1 as teacher by 1.9 points (code) and 2.6 points (math) on the average benchmark score, although R1 is the stronger model.
results.setup: 31,600-example datasets per domain (code, math), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student, same sampling hyperparameters across teachers; Table 8 math: QwQ 44.2 versus R1 41.6; code: 44.2 versus 42.3.
results.quote: yielding an average accuracy improvement of 1.9% and 2.6% over using DeepSeek-R1 as a teacher for code and math, respectively.
results.note: Table 47 (appendix) prints R1 as teacher for code at 38.0 average, not the 42.3 in Table 8; math R1 is 41.6 in Table 8 and 40.6 in Table 48. On the science average R1 is higher than QwQ (49.0 versus 48.0, Table 49) even though the overall average favours QwQ (39.1 versus 35.9).

results.claim: No answer-filtering or verification strategy beat training on all samples, so the final pipeline skips answer filtering.
results.setup: 63,200 answers generated, filtered to 31,600; no-filtering baseline is not compute-controlled (63,200 questions). Math table: no filtering 41.9, random 41.6, GPT verification 40.0, majority consensus 41.0. 7B student, R1 teacher.
results.quote: we opt to skip this part in the following steps of the pipeline.
results.note: Appendix H.1 (Table 15): on the original OpenThinker data, verification hurt at 7B and helped at 32B, so the finding is stated for the 7B student and the 31.6K scale.

results.claim: Verification of the original OpenThoughts-114K data may hurt a 7B model but help a 32B model.
results.setup: OpenThinker-7B 41.9 versus 45.0 unverified; OpenThinker-32B 64.5 versus 62.1 unverified; OpenThoughts-114K data with R1 traces.
results.quote: Our results show that verification may hurt performance at the 7B level but help at the 32B level.

results.claim: Sampling multiple answers per question can enlarge a data source at least 16x, and the scale gives the gains.
results.setup: Dedup (none, fuzzy, exact) crossed with 1x, 4x, 16x sampling at 31,600 examples; for code and science the combinations perform similarly; for math exact dedup with 4x was best and exact dedup with 16x second best and was chosen for scalability.
results.quote: increase the size of a data source by at least 16×.
results.note: Table 42 (math) shows exact dedup with 1x sampling at 41.7 average beating exact dedup 16x at 40.1; the 16x choice rests on scalability, not on a higher score.

results.claim: Mixing only the top two question sources beats mixing many sources.
results.setup: 31,600 questions split evenly over the top N sources, N in 1, 2, 4, 8, 16; code domain Top 2 = 41.3 versus Top 16 = 36.4.

results.claim: The choice of question source moves the average score by 17.2 points between the best and worst code source.
results.setup: 27 code sources, 31,600 questions each, R1 answers, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; StackExchange-CodeGolf 38.8 versus bugdaryan/sql-create-context 21.6.
results.quote: yielding a 17.2 gap between the strongest and the weakest code datasets

results.claim: LLM-based question filters (difficulty for code, response length for math and science) beat random selection by 4% (math) and 6% (code) on average.
results.metric: average accuracy improvement over random filter
results.setup: Code: difficulty-based 43.0 versus random 39.7; math: GPT-4.1-mini response length 41.9 versus random 35.2; 31,600 examples, R1 teacher.
results.quote: resulted in an average improvement of 4% and 6% over the random filtering baseline
results.note: The text order is 'math and code ... 4% and 6%'; the table gaps are about 6.7 points for math and 3.3 for code, which suggests the text may have the domains swapped.

results.claim: Performance on many benchmarks keeps improving up to the 1M dataset size, while AMC23 and MATH500 saturate and HLE does not respond to scale.
results.setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct finetuned on subsets of OpenThoughts3-1.2M from about 316 to 1M; Fig 8 compares with AM, Nemotron Nano, s1.1 and LIMO; curves are not smooth and retraining a fixed dataset did not fully explain dips.
results.quote: Performance on many of the studied benchmarks continues to improve up to the 1M scale.
results.note: A slight drop at 100K on all code benchmarks was traced to the easy LiveCodeBench problems (Appendix I.2).

results.claim: Removing self-reflection words from traces cuts downstream performance by about half (relative 49.1%).
results.setup: 12K-instance OpenThoughts3 subset; removing 'wait'-style keywords cuts average trace length from about 11.6K to 0.3K tokens; baseline average 51.4 versus 26.3.
results.quote: removing self-reflection leads to an average relative performance drop of 49.1%
results.note: Text says 11.6K average length, the Table 22 caption says 11.5K, the table cell 11593.

results.claim: Dropping traces longer than 2048 tokens degrades performance by 33.3% relative; higher thresholds hurt less.
results.setup: Same 12K OpenThoughts3 subset; filter thresholds 2048, 4096, 8192 tokens give averages 34.2, 39.9, 42.3 versus 51.4.

results.claim: Cost: annotating the 1.2M examples with QwQ-32B took 22,000 H100 GPU hours, and one OpenThinker3-7B training run took 25,000 A100 GPU hours.
results.setup: 512 A100 GPUs (128 nodes x 4); annotation on 16 GH200 nodes; annotating one 31,600-example pipeline dataset cost roughly $300 in DeepSeek API fees.
results.quote: One single run of training OpenThinker3-7B required 25,000 A100 GPU hours

results.claim: Reasoning SFT degrades safety: OpenThinker3-7B has a 55.5 Harmbench harmfulness rate against 14.5 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
results.setup: GPT-4o grader, share of maximum-score responses; no safety data in training; lower is better.
results.table: Table 30, row OpenThinker3-7B, column Harmbench; baseline row Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

results.claim: The same OpenThoughts3 data lifts Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct strongly (AMC23 from 15.8 to 75.2), but Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct stays best overall.
results.setup: 100K OpenThoughts3 samples, SFT; Qwen start 86.8 on AMC23.

results.claim: Choosing the shortest of several sampled responses beats the longest by a wide margin on AIME24.
results.setup: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on AIME24; majority vote 76.67, vanilla 55.00; the pattern is model-dependent (Sky-T1-32B differs).
results.quote: the shortest strategy (66.67%) significantly outperforms the longest

results.claim: A Qwen2.5-7B finetuned on R1-annotated Supreme Court opinion classification (majority-verified) reaches 0.819 accuracy against 0.739 for R1 itself.
results.setup: 2K examples annotated 5x by R1 and filtered by majority vote (8.3K of 10K kept); test set 1.52K; unfinetuned Qwen2.5-7B 0.271; single run.
results.table: Table 28, row Qwen2.5-7B finetuned on 2K examples (5x R1-annotated, majority verified), column Accuracy

results.claim: The decontamination scheme misses 12 of 3092 manually contaminated questions and discards 1.4% of clean ones.
results.setup: Test bed of 3092 contaminated and 3000 uncontaminated samples built from MATH500, GPQA Diamond and LiveCodeBench with paraphrase alterations; Indel >= 75% or shared 13-gram.
results.quote: Our final decontamination algorithm only misses 12 questions out of 3092
results.note: The text and Fig 7 caption call 99.6% the 'true negative rate'; with 12 of 3092 missed, 99.6% is the recall of contaminated samples.

limits: The authors did not explore datasets for reinforcement learning, staged SFT or curriculum learning (Section 6).

Strategies were chosen by average over all domains, assuming cross-domain transfer; whether that transfer persists once domains are mixed is open (Section 6 and Appendix H.5, Table 24 shows code-to-science transfer vanished when science data was mixed in).

Pipeline choices rest on one 31,600-example run per strategy with standard errors; sizes above 31.6K were not used to choose strategies, and scaling curves show dips not explained by retraining noise.
Verification and answer filtering findings are for a 7B student; the original OpenThoughts data showed verification helping at 32B (Table 15).
Safety degrades with each OpenThinker generation (Harmbench 36.8, 42.8, 55.5) and no safety data was used.

OpenThinker3-7B trails frontier API models on average (Table 31: Gemini-2.5-pro 69.6) and DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B on most benchmarks (Table 29); Alice-in-Wonderland tests show distilled models fluctuate on structure-preserving variations (Appendix N).

The PDF is arXiv v2 of 5 Jun 2025 and names no venue; the datasets, student and benchmarks (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Evalchemy settings, 2025 competitions) date from spring 2025, before Qwen3 (the authors name it as future work).
Open reproducibility gaps: training sequence length, precision, seeds, teacher sampling settings and training steps are not stated; code is described as 'will be released'.
